title: Experimenting with AI agents to turn my hobby game development into an automated content pipeline.
author: Bishopped
selftext:
I've been working on a hobby game using AI agents pretty extensively, and recently started exploring whether those same tools could help document and share the development process.

For context, I'm not a professional developer. I've always enjoyed systems design, game design and figuring out how things should work, but historically most of my ideas ended up buried in one of my dozens of notebooks.

AI has fundamentally changed what's possible for me as a hobbyist.

The latest experiment has been creating an automated content pipeline around the game's actual development progress.

**The idea**

When a development workstream is completed and its pull request is merged, an AI agent reviews the development diary and relevant changes, then prepares a blog post explaining what happened.

From there, the process follows a series of approval gates:

1. Blog post generated → I review and approve it.
2. Video script generated → I review and approve it.
3. Video draft rendered → I review and approve it.
4. Final video exported → Available for download and manual publication.

There are also two other content formats:

* **Design Ledgers:** Explorations of game design decisions, presented through tactical diagrams, projections and animated interfaces.
* **Incident Reports:** Interesting failures, bugs and unexpected behaviour encountered during development and testing.

The aim is to make the development process itself the source of the content, rather than constantly trying to invent things to post.

**Where things got interesting**

Generating the content turned out to be relatively straightforward, but I had no idea how to make the approval process reliable and easier to manage.

The agents introduced a persistent, versioned review queue in GitHub, alongside automated notifications whenever something needed my attention.

Our first implementation had a fairly amusing flaw: the notification system monitored the same branch it updated when acknowledging an alert, so acknowledging a notification could trigger another execution of the notifier.

We eventually separated the review state from the event that wakes the notifier. Acknowledgments can update the queue without triggering another notification cycle.

After a few iterations, we successfully tested an actual notification appearing in ChatGPT's Scheduled interface.

Seeing that work was honestly one of the most satisfying moments I've had experimenting with AI.

**A word on AI's contribution**

I want to be careful about how I describe this because I see a lot of criticism directed at people using AI who claim to have personally built things.

The agents are doing an enormous amount of the heavy lifting here. They're writing code, investigating failures, proposing implementations, producing graphics, generating narration and rendering videos.

My contribution is primarily direction, design decisions, defining constraints, questioning approaches, testing results and deciding what gets approved.

I'm learning a ridiculous amount through that process, but I don't want to pretend I'm personally implementing everything.

It's a collaboration where the technical execution is heavily AI-assisted, and I'm responsible for steering the work and judging whether the results are actually any good.

**Where it's at now**

The pipeline has successfully produced a complete, narrated video using a reusable holographic tactical interface style, with synchronized captions and background music.

The notification system has also passed its first real delivery test.

Everything still requires explicit approval, and publication remains manual.

There's plenty left to improve, but the fact that this started as a way of documenting a hobby game and has evolved into an experiment in agent orchestration, event-driven automation and media production is pretty wild to me.

I'm particularly interested in how other people are approaching AI-assisted projects like this.

I've uploaded the video explaining this process which was made using the process itself for reference.
